It's not complete, as no prepper kit ever is. I figure that if things really go down in an hand-basket, the one kind of thing that you can't (or don't want to) salvage from scrap is medical supplies.

I approach medical care with a 3 tiered system. All medical components are vacuum sealed (or just sealed) to keep them clean and fresh (just like me). The separate tiers are designed to build on each other so that I am not duplicating supplies (with a few minor exceptions of high use commodities such as bandaids, bug sting kits, etc). No need for a knife ace bandage in each one, just strap them all together. All I'm missing for Tier 3 is a proper bag that I can use which will allow me to pick it up and go, strap it and go, or unstrap it and leave it at camp/base. Additionally, I have two completely identical sets of kits. One for travel, one for home or base.

These kits are intended to be lean and light because running all day with a lot of weight sucks balls.

Tier 1: I got an oopsie.

This tier is your standard first aid kid that is in literally anyone's home. Scrapes, bug stings, minor cuts, pain relievers, x-acto knife.

Tier 2: You mean someone is seriously hurt and needs some help now?

This is a bit more serious. It's strapped to the Tier 1 kit but includes blister pads, tweezers, celox, bandages of all sizes, bandana, and so on. This is pretty much a well stocked first aid kit in anyone's home.

Tier 3: OMFG. Jim, he's dying.

This is my diagnostic and trauma kit: https://files.catbox.moe/ztlca2.jpg

It's small. Where it gets bigger is when I got the 02/airway kit going. The vast majority of trauma can be solved with a stack of gauze, a couple triangular bandages, disinfectant, and a suture kit. Is it pretty? No. But the goal is to hold the blood in. For gunshots to the arms, legs, and chest: a tourniquet and chest seals. I would be cautious of the tourniquet, the far vast majority can't use them even after training. Placement, and the correct tightness is vital. This is where your diagnostic gear shines, you want it right enough to stop the bleeding, but not tight enough to kill the arm.

I think airway could be incorporated into your level two. An NPA is literally a latex straw, and an OPA is a tube 1/2" by 3" long. The reason is that if you get an injury to your face (eg tree branch to the face), you can literally choke on your own blood. When I get home today, I'll grab more photos.

So, full disclosure: I'm a medic on a very small fire department in the middle of butt-fuck nowhere. My level 1 + 02 kit is built for holding victims of car wrecks together for an hour until the ambulance/helicopter shows. The expansion (in the tubs), is for a 48hr ultrarace that I volunteer for (so remote that we're beyond the banjos) where we see just about everything. We routinely see hypo/hyperthermia, drownings, hypo/hyperglycemia, trauma of every type, sprains/strains, dehydration, people spraying each other with bear spray (hilarious for me, not for them). One year we saw a chick throwing blood clots internally. If a prepper (you, me, anyone on here) has to bug out, they will absolutely see all this and more.

My belief is that each prepper group should have an actual medic at EMR / EMT or Wilderness level. It's not enough to do what the army does since we simply don't have helicopters and field hospitals. Literally no one but your buddies care if you die face down in the snow.
